clusters.name: Your stepfather Desmond and your father's separation from Bettina, 1987–1988
clusters.reason: Around 1987, three shifts pile up: your distance from Desmond hardened as a pattern you've carried; your pull toward your father stayed warm even as he and Bettina separated over starting a family; and your own anxiety rose when you made the chess squad and found yourself out of your depth. Your stepmother's departure and return happened in these months, and the strain on the household sits alongside your own struggle.

clusters.name: Your grandfather Gordon's death, 1991–1992
clusters.reason: Your grandfather died in June 1991, and within the year: your anxiety climbed when a wrist injury stopped your playing in the autumn; you and Rafe clashed and he moved out; your functioning dropped as you grew lost and low with him gone and your mother about to remarry; you began getting high and absorbed in fixing radios. Your mother filled in your college forms as you underfunctioned. Around the same time your grandmother Winifred was treated for a thyroid tumour. These shifts—your injury, the conflict with Rafe, your low functioning, and your mother's overfunctioning—cluster around his death and the household upheaval that followed.

clusters.name: Your separation from Joelle, 1999
clusters.reason: In 1999, two shifts that count sit close: your insomnia began getting in the way before concerts though you played well, and you separated from Joelle in the summer. You started with a therapist afterward in August. Your functioning rose as you played the best you ever had that year, but the symptom of insomnia and the relationship shift—the split itself—belong together in these months. No one else's shifts show then.

clusters.name: Your separation from Marisol and your grandmother Winifred's final illness, 2001–2004
clusters.reason: Around 2001 and 2002, multiple shifts pile up: your anxiety and low functioning climbed as you ran out of steam for performing and faced a disastrous audition; your grandmother was found to have bowel cancer and began chemotherapy; you grew distant from family and friends and left Thornbury for Gull Harbour; you met Marisol and moved to Fenwick with her within the year. You split up in October 2003 and sank into deep depression that winter. Back in Thornbury, you could not face your family—your anxiety high and distance deep—yet relied on friends like Corbin, Dale, and Hamish. Your father and Corbin spoke several times during your stay. You returned to your therapist and your functioning began to rise. Your grandmother spent her final months in your parents' home and died in February 2004. These shifts—your burnout, her illness, your relationship collapse, your depression, and the slow turn toward friends and helpers—cluster together across these years.

clusters.name: Your grandmother Lorna's death and your cutoff from your mother, 2008
clusters.reason: Your grandmother Lorna died in early January 2008, and within months: you worked at Alder Creek with Silas and grew too drained for conversation with your mother; she pressed you to visit and you kept the door shut on her; you left for nursing school at Marlow Sound and stopped speaking to her when you moved that summer, a silence that held roughly a year. Your aunt Imogen had a stroke around the same time with months of rehabilitation ahead. The cutoff with your mother, her rising anxiety and your distance, cluster around your grandmother's death and your move away.

clusters.name: Your marriage to Wren and strain in her family, 2017–2019
clusters.reason: Around your marriage to Wren in March 2017, shifts pile up over the following two and a half years: your contact with your mother eased off slightly once Wren came along; your cousin Alice was diagnosed with multiple sclerosis; your sister Tara married and settled in Rennick for her airline work; your aunt Imogen's memory slipped and worsened, and she began lashing out when muddled. By October 2019, Wren grew swamped with events—a street party, a fundraiser, her mother's retirement—and your anxiety rose as you overfunctioned laying out plans to settle her; her family talks all day and nothing happens to one that the others don't hear; you awoke from the small hours at the lake weekend with no more sleep, felt you didn't belong, and grew distant from the group. Your sleep is at its worst around her family. These shifts in Wren's anxiety and functioning, the tight fusion in her family, your own symptom and distance, and the strain between you cluster around your marriage and intensify as her family's demands mount.
